newsitem.title: UK: FAO says African nations still face food shortages.
newsitem.headline: FAO says African nations still face food shortages.

text.p: Thirteen African countries are suffering from continued food shortages despite improved crop and food supplies in much of sub-Saharan Africa, the UN Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) said in a report.

"Unless exceptional food assistance allocations are made, it is probable that a number of African countries will face increased hardship as many of their people will not be able to find enough food to eat," said Abdur Rashid, chief of the FAO Global Information and Eary Warning System.

Worst-hit are Burundi, Liberia and Somalia according to the special FAO quarterly report on food and crops in sub-Saharan Africa issued here just over a month before the World Food Summit at FAO's Rome headquarters.
A sharp drop in food production in Liberia is causing pockets of famine with severe malnutrition and starvation in several regions where food aid was disrupted by civil strife.
Likewise food supplies have been threatened in Burundi where prices have risen sharply since July.
A volatile political situation in Somalia has made the food supply in Somalia and Sudan precarious, it noted.
Also facing shortages are Angola, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Rwanda, Sierre Leone and Zaire.

About 40 percent of the total population of sub-Saharan Africa, or some 215 million people, are already chronically undernourished and FAO said this number could rise to 265 million by the year 2010 unless actiuon is taken.
Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for half the 82 nations listed by the FAO as low-income food-deficit countries.

But in contrast FAO said in Southern Africa crops showed a "marked improvement" with an estimated 1995/96 coarse grains crop of 19.8 million tonnes - some 89 percent up on the previous year's drought-hit crop and 40 percent above average. The total 1996 southern African cereal crop is put at 24 million tonnes of 65 percent up on last year and 35 percent above average.
